Walmart vs. Coca-Cola: 53 and 64 Straight Years of Raises. Which Dividend Grows Faster From Here? ©Leung Cho Pan and Wavebreakmedia from Getty Images Pro via Canva
Key Takeaways

Walmart yields 0.8% and Coca-Cola 2.3%, and both raised their dividends again this year.

Walmart's dividend takes 57% of its free cash flow over the trailing 12 months, against 79% for Coca-Cola.

Coca-Cola's free cash flow fell short of its dividend in 2024 and 2025 before recovering, and the company raised its 2026 free cash flow guidance in October.

$10,000 in Walmart pays $80 a year today against $230 from Coca-Cola, and at their five-year growth rates, Walmart's income wouldn't catch up for more than 30 years.

If you want a dividend that goes up every year, Walmart (WMT:NASDAQ) and Coca-Cola (KO:NYSE) are about as dependable as it gets. Both have also given income investors good news lately. Walmart raised its full-year guidance in August, and Coca-Cola raised its free cash flow outlook in October.

But if you're counting on those raises, their size matters as much as their streak. So which of these dividends should grow faster from here?

6 safe dividend stocks paying retirees 6%+ yields

There are over 100 stocks paying 6%+ annual dividends today.

But after an extensive investment review leveraging TIKR's proprietary data, we now believe only six of them are truly safe for retirees.

They're all yours for free as part of our new investment report, which you can access right here.

Walmart keeps its payout small

Walmart's growth is coming from a lot more than store shelves. In its second quarter, the three months to July 31, 2026, revenue rose 5.9% to $187.9 billion and operating income jumped 28.8% (17.4% adjusted, at constant currency) from a year earlier. Global e-commerce sales grew 23%, advertising 38% and membership fee revenue 17%.

Walmart is putting a lot of that money back into prices. "We're investing heavily in price because customers need us to and because we believe it drives market share gains over time," CEO John Furner said on the second-quarter call.

The dividend leaves plenty of room for that spending. Free cash flow covered it comfortably in each of the last 10 fiscal years, and dividends took 50.3% of it in fiscal 2026, the year ended January 2026:

Walmart (WMT): free cash flow vs. common dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2017–2026 (years to January) (TIKR)

Over the 12 months to July 31, 2026, its cash dividend payout ratio is a well-covered 57%. Costs are the main risk. Walmart expects more than $2 billion of extra fuel costs this year beyond what its original guidance assumed. Its free cash flow for the six months to July 31 fell $1.4 billion from a year earlier, to $5.5 billion.

Coca-Cola's cash is back

Coca-Cola pays out a much bigger share of its cash than Walmart, and its record shows the strain. Its dividend payments rose every year from 2016 to 2025, from $6.04 billion to $8.78 billion. But free cash flow fell short of them in four of those 10 years, including 2024 and 2025:

title: How These 5 Big-Box Retailers Compete for the Same Shopper

How These 5 Big-Box Retailers Compete for the Same Shopper
Thomas Niel, The Motley Fool

LOW
COST

HD

Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT), Costco Wholesale (NASDAQ: COST), Target (NYSE: TGT), Home Depot (NYSE: HD), and Lowe's Companies (NYSE: LOW) are all after the same thing: a large share of household budgets. They just go about it in different ways. While all five of these big-box retailers may sell home and garden products, only the last two specialize in them. In the case of the first three, each one also sells everyday consumer staple items, like food, clothing, and household goods.

Yet while Walmart in particular may be "crushing it" right now, the strengths of these other four names are nothing to sneeze at. In fact, considering other factors, like valuation, it may not necessarily be the leaders of the pack that are among the best retail stocks to buy.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images
1. Walmart keeps gaining ground, but tread carefully

Walmart reports quarterly earnings later this month. Analysts may anticipate relatively little earnings growth this quarter, but the retail giant could beat expectations if ongoing trends hold. In August, when the omnichannel retailer last reported earnings, the company touted continued market share gains across all income groups, particularly high-income households.

The company also reported strong e-commerce growth, with this segment's revenue growing 24% year over year. Based on these metrics, one could argue that Walmart is competing for household budget market share through both low prices and high convenience, with the success of its Walmart+ platform playing a major role in driving this growth.

Still, while Walmart touted many metrics in its Q2 earnings release, investors reacted negatively to lower-than-expected same-store sales and guidance updates that fell short of forecasts. Shares have recovered since pulling back after earnings, yet with the stock trading at 46 times forward earnings, a big premium to most of its big-box competition, any sort of hiccup or slip-up with Q3 results could trigger the next big sell-off.

2. Customer loyalty keeps Costco humming along, yet valuation is still concerning

Costco doesn't release quarterly results until December. However, thanks to the discount retail club's monthly releases of sales and related metrics, investors can more quickly get a sense of how the company is currently performing. On Nov. 4, Costco released its October 2026 sales results. Excluding the impact of higher gas prices and currency fluctuations, the company reported year-over-year comparable sales growth of 7.3%, with U.S. comparable sales rising 8.1% compared to the prior year's month. Digital sales were up 22.5% compared to October 2025.

title: The Kiplinger Dividend 15: Our Favorite Dividend-Paying Stocks

Credit: Getty Images

Please, spare a few thoughts for pitiable dividend-paying companies and the souls who invest in them. Interest rates are rising, rather than falling, leaving most dividend payouts struggling to compete with the robust yields of bonds. Even Treasuries look good. And the stock market? The belles of the ball once again are hot, growthy tech firms. Stodgy dividend payers are the wallflowers.

Or, just maybe, the picture is a bit more complex. No matter how juicy the yield, bonds have duration risk — the risk that prices will fall as rates rise. Dividend-paying stocks can be a port in the storm if market sentiment becomes more bearish.

For now, though, the Kiplinger Dividend 15, the list of our favorite dividend-paying stocks, has underwhelmed. Over the past 12 months, the Dividend 15 (now in its 10th year) gained 4.5%, on average, badly trailing the 15.7% total return in the S&P 500 index. There were winners, to be sure, led by Johnson & Johnson's (JNJ) 45.6% return. Three others — U.S. Bancorp (USB), Enterprise Products Partners (EPD) and Emerson Electric (EMR) — outperformed. But two legends of consumer spending, McDonald's (MCD) and Home Depot (HD), dragged down the bunch with losses of 21.6% and 27.5%, respectively.

Our methodology for finding the best dividend-paying stocks

We divide our favorites into three categories. The stalwarts are steady payers that have racked up decades of consistent dividend hikes. The dividend growers boast sizable payout hikes every year and are typically increasing their rate of dividend growth. Members of the high-yielders are high-quality stocks that offer big dividends. The average yield for the Dividend 15 as a whole is 2.5%, nearly two and a half times the 1.1% yield of the S&P 500.

Five stocks on the list — McKesson (MCK), Mastercard (MA), Broadcom (AVGO), Walmart (WMT) and our brand-new member, Amphenol (APH) — have yields below the S&P 500 average, with four on the list for their dividend growth. The 15 members increased their dividend by an average of 8.2% over the past 12 months compared with the previous year.

This year, we're removing Home Depot from the list, replacing it with electrical- and electronic-component manufacturer Amphenol. Home Depot's sales and profits have stalled along with the U.S. housing market. That has led the board to rein in dividend boosts: The payout increased only 1.5% in the past year, woefully short of the consistent double-digit growth we look for.

title: Jensen Huang’s net worth drops $6.5 billion as Nvidia stock slides in the fallout of spy affair scandal investigation
detail:
Jensen Huang’s net worth drops $6.5 billion as Nvidia stock slides in the fallout of spy affair scandal investigation
Emma Burleigh
Tue, November 10, 2026 at 8:40 AM MST 4 min read
NVDA
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

New probes into Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy have sent Nvidia stock sliding this week—and now, the billionaire CEO is no longer one of the 10 richest people in the world as his wealth continues to slide down the rankings.

The day after the Nvidia cofounder confirmed he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, his wealth dropped by $6.5 billion. Meanwhile, his company's stock fell by as much as 9% by Monday, winding up 4.3% lower at $178.67 per share. 

Huang owns around 870 million shares (roughly 3.5%) of the $4.3 trillion business in his own name and family trusts, according to a September 2026 filing, which represents the bulk of his fortune.

The loss has sent him tumbling down the ultra-rich list past Walmart heirs Jim Walton and Rob Walton, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. 

But Huang is still worth a whopping $148 billion and is the 12th wealthiest person in the world. 

Fortune has reached out to Nvidia for comment. 

Further investigations and lawsuits could continue to impact Nvidia's stock and Huang's net worth 

Investors and the public alike are reeling from the most recent investigations into Huang's alleged spy affair scandal. Last month, the New York Times reported that the CEO had formed a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which buys Nvidia's AI chips. 

On Sunday, Nvidia's board launched an independent investigation into the reports that Huang had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort," and the CEO sent an email to staffers apologizing for the extramarital affair. And just yesterday, Rosen Law firm filed a class-action lawsuit in federal court alleging that the company and its CEO failed to disclose information about Huang's connections to the alleged Chinese spy accused of passing information to Beijing. 

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," Nvidia's board of directors said in a statement. "Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it."

The latest dip in Huang's wealth only compounded upon pre-existing problems, as the CEO briefly dropped out of the top 10 last week after a broad tech stock sell-off following the Democrats' midterm victories. 

But the pending investigations and lawsuits could continue to impact Nvidia's stock and Huang's net worth. 

Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, wrote in a research note that this is a "black eye moment" for the CEO and will create "an overhang" on the company's stock. There are a myriad of concerns as Huang has an outsized influence on the company, U.S.-China tensions rage on, and the possible tighter export restrictions loom overhead.

title: Walmart's Sam's Club Sees Higher Traffic: Can Momentum Last?

Walmart's Sam's Club Sees Higher Traffic: Can Momentum Last?

Trading disclosure

Walmart Inc. WMT continues to see encouraging transaction growth at its Sam's Club U.S. business, supported by expanding membership and digital convenience. The warehouse club format is benefiting from higher shopping volumes across key merchandise categories, while growing adoption of digital services is providing additional support. These trends highlight the importance of member engagement in sustaining sales momentum.

In second-quarter fiscal 2027, Sam's Club U.S. transactions increased 7% compared with 3.9% growth in the year-ago quarter. Comparable sales, excluding fuel, rose 4.4%, driven by higher transactions and unit volumes, with strength across grocery and general merchandise. However, average ticket declined 2.5% against 2% growth a year earlier.

Membership trends remained favorable. Membership fee revenues increased 6%, reflecting steady growth in member counts and higher Plus membership penetration. Gen Z and millennials accounted for more than half of new member sign-ups, with Plus penetration exceeding 50% among this group.

Digital capabilities are also contributing to the business's momentum. Sam's Club U.S. eCommerce sales grew 26%, representing approximately 20% of net sales, excluding fuel. Club-fulfilled delivery recorded triple-digit growth following the April launch of one-hour delivery. Meanwhile, Scan & Go adoption improved approximately 110 basis points.

Looking ahead, the key consideration is whether stronger transaction volumes can continue supporting comparable sales amid declining average ticket values. While membership growth and digital adoption remain encouraging, comparable-sales growth moderated from 5.9% a year earlier. Sustained transaction growth, alongside improved basket values, would provide a stronger foundation for Sam's Club's sales momentum.

What Do the Latest Metrics Say About Walmart?

Walmart, which competes with Costco Wholesale Corporation COST and Target Corporation TGT, has seen its shares gain 22.7% over the past year compared with the industry's growth of 21.4%. Costco shares have climbed 16.5%, while Target has surged 82.9% in the aforementioned period.

Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) delivered a third-quarter earnings report that strengthened its cloud growth story. AWS grew 39% year over year, its fastest growth in nearly 5 years. As long as the cloud engine speeds up like this, the growth case stays intact.

ollo / Getty Images
Why AWS Acceleration Drives the Amazon Growth Case

AWS is Amazon's profit engine, and it keeps speeding up as it gets bigger. Growth ran 24% in Q4 2025, 28% in Q1, 37% in Q2 and 39% in Q3. Q3 revenue reached $45.98B, and AWS operating income climbed to $17.77B from $11.43B a year earlier.

The runway looks long. AWS carries a $578 billion backlog, and Bedrock token volume rose nearly 17x. CEO Andy Jassy said "We believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 and 2028 and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years."

Three Numbers Powering Amazon's Momentum

First, margins. Consolidated operating margin hit 13.9%, the company's highest ever, and operating income rose 61.15% to $28.08B, even with a Prime Day calendar shift reducing retail growth by roughly 400 bps.

Second, custom silicon. The chips business grew at triple-digit percentages, Graviton and Trainium commitments rose more than 20x, and customers saved more than $2 billion in Q3 alone. Owning the chip brings down AWS's cost structure for years.

What Moved Best Buy Stock?

Best Buy (BBY) shares rose 6.7% on Monday, November 9, 2026, outpacing the S&P 500's 2.3% gain. The company issued no announcement, earnings report or filing around the move. The advance occurred on a day Wall Street rebounded from a steep sell-off in global technology stocks the week before, with the Nasdaq Composite up 2.7%. So what has been happening in Best Buy's own business?

Computing Led Best Buy's Latest Sales Growth

In the fiscal second quarter of 2027, which ended August 1, 2026, Best Buy's revenue rose 3.6% from a year earlier. Management said on the August 27 call that computing growth led the way. Home theater was the second-biggest driver, and sales of newer categories such as AI glasses and trading cards more than doubled.

Some of that technology now costs shoppers more. Management said industry-wide memory cost increases were raising product costs, with higher prices flowing into its assortment. In computing, the average selling price rose by a mid-teens percentage in the quarter, while units fell by a high single digit. Management described customers who are still spending, but remain value-focused and attracted to sales moments.

Retail Rose Too, But Best Buy Rose More

Best Buy moved the same way as its sector and its peers that day, but further. The SPDR consumer discretionary sector fund, XLY, rose 2.9%, and all four of the other companies on the Trefis peer list for Best Buy rose too. Target gained 4.0% and Walmart 0.1%. Amazon and Home Depot each gained 2.9%. So Best Buy rose with its group, by more than twice as much as the sector fund.

Best Buy Stock Closed At A One-Year High

The $106.28 close on November 9 was Best Buy's highest of the past year. Gains this large are not new for the stock. It posted three rises at least this big in the prior 365 days, most recently an 8.0% gain on November 4.

Over the past twelve months the stock returned 42.3%, against 13.7% for the S&P 500. The climb began after a low in May: Best Buy's lowest close of the past year was $55.52, on May 13. Over the six months from May 11, a window that takes in that low, the stock returned 88.9%, against 2.4% for the index. At the November 9 close, Best Buy traded at 0.53 times its sales over the past twelve months, against 3.1 times for the S&P 500. On earnings the gap is far smaller: 17.7 times against 21.8 times.

Best Buy is expected to report its fiscal third quarter of 2027 later in November 2026. Comparable sales growth, which management guided to 1% to 3% for that quarter, is the measure to watch.
